qs.q: A 27-year-old woman attends her first antenatal care visit at 10 weeks gestation. According to the World Health Organization recommendations for an uncomplicated routine pregnancy, what is the minimum recommended number of antenatal contacts?
qs.e: The World Health Organization recommends a minimum of eight antenatal contacts for uncomplicated routine pregnancies to optimize maternal and fetal outcomes. Early booking within the first trimester is also advised.
qs.s: Obstetrics: Normal Pregnancy and Antenatal Care: MCQs

qs.q: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification, which specific astrocytoma is categorized as Grade IV?
qs.e: Glioblastoma is classified by the WHO as a Grade IV astrocytoma and represents the majority of high-grade astrocytomas. Pilocytic astrocytomas are Grade I, diffuse astrocytomas are Grade II, and anaplastic astrocytomas are Grade III.

qs.q: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria, anemia is defined as a hemoglobin level lower than which threshold in adult women?
qs.e: The WHO defines anemia as a hemoglobin level lower than 12 g/dL in women and 13 g/dL in men. Thresholds below or above these do not match the standard WHO reference criteria provided.

qs.q: What is the primary characteristic defining osteoporosis according to the World Health Organization and the National Osteoporosis Foundation?
o: Excessive osteoblastic proliferation leading to dense bones
Primary accumulation of adipocytes within the cortical layer
Softening of bone due to defective mineralization of matrix
Low bone mass and micro-architectural deterioration of tissue
qs.e: Osteoporosis is defined as a disease characterized by low bone mass and micro-architectural deterioration of bone tissue. Softening of the bone is instead characteristic of osteomalacia.

qs.q: According to the World Health Organization, how is Helicobacter pylori classified regarding its carcinogenic potential?
qs.e: H. pylori is classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen due to its association with gastric cancer. It is not placed in lower risk categories.
qs.s: Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old traveler returns from Southeast Asia with acute febrile illness, petechiae, a platelet count of 80,000/uL, and hemoconcentration. Which condition fulfills the World Health Organization diagnostic criteria?
qs.e: Dengue hemorrhagic fever requires fever, hemorrhagic manifestations, thrombocytopenia below 100,000/uL, and objective evidence of plasma leakage. Dengue shock syndrome requires these same criteria plus clinical evidence of circulatory failure.

es.q: Discuss the pre-operative, intra-operative, and post-operative World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for the prevention of surgical site infections.
es.m:
- **Pre-operative bathing and decolonisation:** Patients should bathe or shower with plain or antimicrobial soap; decolonise *S. aureus* carriers with mupirocin nasal ointment and chlorhexidine body wash before cardiac and orthopaedic surgery.
- **Hair removal restrictions:** Do not remove hair unless essential; if needed, clip rather than shave on the day of surgery to avoid razors causing micro-trauma.
- **Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis timing:** Administer prophylaxis within 120 minutes before the incision (ideally within 60 minutes) guided by drug half-life as a single dose using agents like cefazolin or cefuroxime, and do not continue post-operatively.

ai.title: World Health Organization Paediatrics Guidelines
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: WHO paediatric guidance focuses on child growth, nutrition, immunisation, and disease control in low‑resource settings. It provides evidence‑based thresholds, diagnostic criteria and management pathways for common childhood illnesses.

sections.p: WHO paediatrics refers to the body of evidence‑based recommendations for child health, including growth standards, immunisation schedules and disease control programmes.
b: WHO growth charts (z‑scores)
Standardised immunisation schedules
Disease‑specific diagnostic criteria

sections.p: WHO classifies severity of common paediatric conditions using simple clinical criteria that can be applied without advanced investigations.
b: Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) – weight‑for‑height <70% or MUAC <11.5 cm
Pneumonia severity – tachypnoea, chest indrawing
Malaria severity – danger signs such as unconsciousness, vomiting, dehydration

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the leading causes of morbidity and mortality are infections, malnutrition and preventable diseases.
b: Infections – malaria, pneumonia, diarrhoea, HIV
Malnutrition – protein‑energy malnutrition, micronutrient deficiencies
Preventable diseases – vaccine‑preventable infections

sections.p: Clinical presentation follows WHO symptom checklists, focusing on observable signs that guide immediate management.
b: Pneumonia – rapid breathing, chest indrawing, nasal flaring
Diarrhoea – frequent loose stools, dehydration signs
SAM – oedema, thin limbs, stunted growth

sections.p: WHO recommends a minimal set of investigations that are feasible in low‑resource settings.

t.b: Detects Plasmodium antigens; a positive result confirms malaria and guides antimalarial therapy
Assesses anaemia; a value <10 g/dL in children indicates need for transfusion or iron therapy
Identifies moderate (11.5–12.5 cm) or severe (<11.5 cm) malnutrition; guides therapeutic feeding
Distinguishes bacterial pharyngitis from viral causes; a positive result justifies antibiotic use

sections.p: Certain signs indicate urgent referral or higher mortality risk.
b: Unconsciousness, seizures, severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, chest indrawing, severe pallor, hypoxaemia

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitoring.
b: Malaria – artemisinin‑based combination therapy; avoid quinine in pregnancy
Pneumonia – first‑line antibiotics (amoxicillin or cotrimoxazole); oxygen if SpO2 <90%
SAM – therapeutic feeding (RUTF), zinc, vitamin A, treat infections

sections.p: Regular growth monitoring, immunisation, nutrition counselling and community health education are key.
b: Monthly growth checks using WHO charts
Routine immunisations per schedule
Micronutrient supplementation (iron, vitamin A)
Pneumonia vs bronchiolitis – both present with tachypnoea but chest indrawing is more typical of pneumonia
SAM vs kwashiorkor – oedema present in both but protein‑energy malnutrition is broader

sections.p: Some tests may give false negatives or positives due to low sensitivity or operator error.
b: Rapid malaria tests may miss low parasitaemia; confirm with microscopy if available
MUAC may be inaccurate in oedematous children; use weight‑for‑height instead
Severe dehydration with inability to keep fluids down
Unconsciousness or seizures
Severe pallor or hypoxaemia
Chest indrawing with tachypnoea >50 breaths/min in children <5 years

faq.q: What is the WHO growth chart z‑score threshold for severe acute malnutrition?
faq.a: Weight‑for‑height z‑score <‑3 or MUAC <11.5 cm indicates severe acute malnutrition.

faq.q: Which antibiotic is first‑line for uncomplicated pneumonia in children?
faq.a: Amoxicillin or cotrimoxazole for 5 days, unless contraindicated.

faq.q: How often should a child be screened for malaria in endemic areas?
faq.a: Monthly screening during peak transmission or if symptomatic; otherwise routine screening is not required.

exam: A 3‑year‑old presents with cough, rapid breathing and chest indrawing. What is the next best step? — Assess SpO2; if <90% give oxygen; start amoxicillin; refer if danger signs present.
A child with fever and diarrhoea has a MUAC of 10.8 cm. What is the WHO classification and management? — Moderate acute malnutrition; give therapeutic feeding, zinc, vitamin A, treat infection.
A 6‑month‑old is brought with a rash and fever. Which vaccine is likely responsible? — Measles vaccine; check for post‑vaccination rash and treat supportive.
A child with cough and nasal flaring but no chest indrawing. What is the likely diagnosis? — Viral upper respiratory infection; no antibiotics needed.
A 2‑year‑old with severe pallor and lethargy. What investigation is most urgent? — Point‑of‑care hemoglobin; if <10 g/dL consider transfusion.
A child with fever and a positive rapid malaria test is started on artemisinin‑based therapy. What is a common adverse effect to monitor? — Liver enzyme elevation; monitor LFTs if available.
